title: 2 Chronicles 20:1–12
context: 2 Chronicles 20:1–12 tells how Moab, Ammon, and others come against Jehoshaphat, and how he and all Judah seek the LORD. Textual note: in 20:1 the WEB reads Meunites, following the ancient Greek translation, while the Hebrew text reads Ammonites at that point; since the children of Ammon are already named in the verse, the WEB follows the Greek reading here, and this draft does not reconstruct the text further. Messengers report a great multitude at Hazazon Tamar, which the text identifies with En Gedi (20:2); En Gedi is commonly placed on the western shore of the Dead Sea, and the relation of this Hazazon Tamar to the one in Genesis 14:7 is discussed. Jehoshaphat proclaims a fast, and Judah gathers to seek help from the LORD. His prayer (20:5–12) is kept here as one unit. It confesses God’s rule over the nations, recalls the gift of the land to the offspring of Abraham, appeals to the promise attached to the temple (compare Solomon’s prayer in 2 Chronicles 6:20, 28, 34), recalls that Israel was not permitted to take the land of Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir (compare Deuteronomy 2:4–5, 9, 19), and ends, “We don’t know what to do, but our eyes are on you.” This chapter has no parallel in Kings. Both traditions read the prayer as shared ground: helpless dependence on the LORD is the right response to overwhelming danger.

verses.text: After this, the children of Moab, the children of Ammon, and with them some of the Meunites, came against Jehoshaphat to battle.
verses.arminianNotes:
After this, Moab, Ammon, and some of the Meunites come against Jehoshaphat to battle. The WEB follows the ancient Greek reading Meunites here, where the Hebrew text reads Ammonites, as noted in the context.

Arminian readers note that the faithful reforms of chapter 19 are followed by a crisis, and they see in this a reminder that faithfulness does not exempt God’s people from danger.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the invasion as a test that will reveal where Judah’s confidence lies, and they note that the large forces of chapter 17 will play no part in the deliverance that follows.

Both traditions read the verse as narrative setting and treat it as shared ground, without building anything on the textual question.

verses.text: Then some came who told Jehoshaphat, saying, “A great multitude is coming against you from beyond the sea from Syria. Behold, they are in Hazazon Tamar” (that is, En Gedi).
verses.arminianNotes:
Messengers tell Jehoshaphat that a great multitude is coming from beyond the sea, and that they are in Hazazon Tamar, which the text identifies as En Gedi. En Gedi is commonly placed on the western shore of the Dead Sea, so the sea is often taken to be the Dead Sea, though the geography is discussed.

Arminian readers see a real and urgent danger close to Judah.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the threat comes from several nations at once, and they see the narrative emphasizing Judah’s helplessness. The relation of this Hazazon Tamar to the one in Genesis 14:7 is discussed and left open.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground and hold the site identifications with appropriate caution.

verses.text: Jehoshaphat was alarmed, and set himself to seek the LORD. He proclaimed a fast throughout all Judah.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoshaphat is alarmed, sets himself to seek the LORD, and proclaims a fast throughout all Judah. Fear turns into prayer.

Arminian readers note that the king chooses to respond to fear by seeking God rather than by turning to allies, a contrast with his alliance with Ahab, and they see the fast as a real and willing act of humility.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God working in the king’s heart so that alarm becomes seeking, and they note that Chronicles regularly presents seeking the LORD as the mark of a faithful king (compare 17:4; 19:3).

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground: fear rightly leads God’s people to seek him, and fasting expresses humble dependence.

verses.text: Judah gathered themselves together to seek help from the LORD. They came out of all the cities of Judah to seek the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
Judah gathers to seek help from the LORD, coming from all the cities of Judah to seek the LORD. The whole nation joins the king.

Arminian readers see a united and willing response of the people, who choose to seek God together, and they note the effect of the teaching mission and reforms in preparing them for this moment.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the repetition of seeking in the verse, which stresses the people’s dependence on the LORD alone, and they see a community turned toward God by his grace in a time of crisis.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about corporate prayer and treat it as a model for God’s people facing danger.

verses.text: Jehoshaphat stood in the assembly of Judah and Jerusalem, in the LORD’s house, before the new court;
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoshaphat stands in the assembly of Judah and Jerusalem in the LORD’s house, before the new court. The prayer begins in the temple.

Arminian readers note that the king leads the people in prayer publicly, and they see the setting as an expression of trust that God hears prayer offered toward his house, as Solomon had asked (compare 2 Chronicles 6:34).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the king prays as a leader of God’s covenant people at the place where God placed his name, and they see the prayer as an act of faith resting on God’s promises rather than on human strength. The meaning of the new court is not explained.

Both traditions read the setting as shared ground.

verses.text: and he said, “LORD, the God of our fathers, aren’t you God in heaven? Aren’t you ruler over all the kingdoms of the nations? Power and might are in your hand, so that no one is able to withstand you.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoshaphat begins, addressing the LORD, the God of their fathers, as God in heaven and ruler over all the kingdoms of the nations, in whose hand are power and might, so that no one can withstand him.

Arminian readers see the prayer grounded in God’s greatness, and they note that confidence in God’s power gives the people reason to trust him rather than despair.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the confession of God’s sovereign rule over all the kingdoms, and they see the prayer beginning, as biblical prayers often do, with who God is before asking what he will do.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground: God’s rule over the nations is the foundation of the people’s hope in this crisis.

verses.text: Didn’t you, our God, drive out the inhabitants of this land before your people Israel, and give it to the offspring of Abraham your friend forever?
verses.arminianNotes:
He recalls that God drove out the inhabitants of the land before Israel and gave it “to the offspring of Abraham your friend forever”. The phrase about Abraham as God’s friend appears also in Isaiah 41:8 and is echoed in James 2:23.

Arminian readers see the people appealing to God’s past faithfulness and to his relationship with Abraham as grounds for trust.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the land was God’s gift, not Israel’s achievement, and they see the appeal to the promise to Abraham as a plea resting on God’s covenant faithfulness.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about remembering God’s promises in prayer, and neither builds a contrast on the phrase.

verses.text: They lived in it, and have built you a sanctuary in it for your name, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
The people lived in the land and built a sanctuary there for God’s name. The prayer recalls the building of the temple.

Arminian readers note that the people’s building of the sanctuary was a response of worship to God’s gift of the land, and they see the temple as a sign of the relationship God had invited them into and they had embraced.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the sanctuary was built for God’s name, which stresses that the temple existed for his glory and as the place where he chose to be called upon, so that the prayer appeals to God’s own honor.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground leading into the appeal to Solomon’s prayer in the next verse.

verses.text: ‘If evil comes on us—the sword, judgment, pestilence, or famine—we will stand before this house, and before you (for your name is in this house), and cry to you in our affliction, and you will hear and save.’
verses.arminianNotes:
The prayer cites the people’s resolve that if evil comes, whether sword, judgment, pestilence, or famine, they will stand before this house and before God, whose name is in it, and cry to him in affliction, and he will hear and save. This echoes Solomon’s prayer (compare 2 Chronicles 6:28, 34).

Arminian readers see the people taking God at his word.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the prayer resting on God’s own promise attached to the temple (compare 7:14–15), and they note that the confidence expressed is in God’s faithfulness to hear.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground: God’s people may cry to him in distress, trusting that he hears and saves.

verses.text: Now, behold, the children of Ammon and Moab and Mount Seir, whom you would not let Israel invade when they came out of the land of Egypt, but they turned away from them, and didn’t destroy them;
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoshaphat names the invaders, Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir, whom God did not let Israel invade when they came out of Egypt, so that Israel turned away from them and did not destroy them. The law records this restraint (compare Deuteronomy 2:4–5, 9, 19).

Arminian readers note that Israel had shown restraint in obedience to God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the appeal as a plea for God to vindicate his own earlier command, since the nations Israel spared now seek to drive Israel out, and they note that the prayer leaves judgment to God.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground and treat the historical appeal as part of a humble and honest prayer.

verses.text: behold, how they reward us, to come to cast us out of your possession, which you have given us to inherit.
verses.arminianNotes:
The prayer says, behold how they reward us, coming to cast us out of your possession, which you have given us to inherit. The land is described as God’s possession.

Arminian readers see the people appealing to God’s justice against ingratitude and aggression, and they note that the prayer brings real grievances to God rather than taking matters into their own hands.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the phrase about God’s possession, noting that the land belongs to God and that Judah holds it as an inheritance from him, so that the threat is against God’s own gift and purpose.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about bringing injustice to God in prayer and trusting him to act.

verses.text: Our God, will you not judge them? For we have no might against this great company that comes against us. We don’t know what to do, but our eyes are on you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The prayer ends, “Our God, will you not judge them? For we have no might against this great company that comes against us. We don’t know what to do, but our eyes are on you.”

Arminian readers see an honest confession of weakness and a willing, trusting dependence on God, and they note that the people choose to look to God rather than to any human source of help.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the climax of the prayer in the confession that Judah has no might, despite the great forces of chapter 17, and they see this helplessness as the setting in which God’s grace is displayed.

Both traditions read the closing words as shared ground and as one of Scripture’s clearest models of dependent prayer in crisis.
